From: Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.ai>
To: Sam Li <sam.li@acme.com>, Jared Miller <jared.miller@acme.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Dylan Brooks <dylan_brooks@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Post-call: integration recap + next steps

Sam/Jared — Neha from Infra/Platform here. I pulled together pointed answers to each of your questions below. If anything needs deeper config examples I can drop a short notebook.

1) SDK / Auth:
- OAuth 2.0: Yes, for Redwood Private we support OAuth 2.0 client credentials (we can integrate with Azure AD). The Private control plane can be configured to accept tokens issued by your IdP and map them to RBAC identities.
- Key rotation / KMS: For hosted, API keys are standard (rotate via Console). For Dedicated/Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for service secret encryption; key rotation can be automated via the control plane.
- Recommendation: For production, use short-lived tokens + our refresh flow or federated tokens via your IdP; we can send best-practice config snippets for Azure AD if you want.

2) Routing & models:
- Per-request model choice: yes, include model=<model_name> in the SDK request (same way as the examples in the quickstart).
- Fallbacks & policy: you can define routing policies (in Console or via API) such as prefer_low_latency then fallback to high_quality. The request can include metadata (route_hint: "low_latency" or "quality"), or you can pin model name explicitly.
- Example header: X-Redwood-Route: low_latency; the control plane enforces policy and does automatic fallback on capacity/timeout.

3) Structured output & tool calling:
- Function/tool calling: we support structured function calls (similar to OpenAI-style function calling). You can declare a JSON schema for expected output (fields, types) and the model will attempt to conform.
- Malformed JSON handling: SDK provides a "schema_validation" flag — if enabled, responses are validated server-side and you'll get a validation result (valid/partial/invalid) in the response envelope. For partial/invalid, we include the raw model_text and a structured diff explaining missing/malformed fields, and we can optionally retry with a clarification prompt.
- Best practice: define tight schemas for high-stakes data and use a small reranking pass (or a deterministic post-processor) to correct bracket/escape issues.

4) Embeddings & rerankers:
- Typical pattern: use Redwood embeddings for first-stage vector search (cosine/dot) + a cross-encoder reranker for final scoring. We offer both: hosted vector search + embeddings, and a managed reranker (lightweight cross-encoder) as an add-on.
- Dimensions: common dims are 512/768/1536 depending on model family; pick the embedding dim that matches the Redwood model you choose for better alignment.
- Normalization & ANN settings: normalize vectors (L2) before cosine search, use HNSW with ef_search tuned for recall (ef_search 64-200 depending on latency). We'll share tuning presets for typical KB sizes (10k, 100k, 1M docs).
- Reranker guidance: rerank top-N (N=100 recommended) with a cross-encoder; if latency is critical, consider a lightweight re-ranker or optimized quantized model in Dedicated.

5) Chat vs completions, tokenization, max_tokens, stop, streaming:
- Chat vs completions: chat endpoints accept a messages array (role/content pairs) and handle conversational system/assistant/user token accounting. Completions accept a prompt string. Tokenization differences are small (same tokenizer family) but chat messages include metadata overhead (role names, separators) so budget slightly less as prompts grow.
- max_tokens: applies to the response (generation) length. For chat, max_tokens counts generated tokens only. You should reserve room for expected response + any safety/finetune tokens. Example: if model max context is 4096 and your prompt+history is 3000 tokens, max_tokens <= 1096.
- stop sequences: supported for completions via stop parameter (list of strings). For chat, stop behaves similarly but we recommend using function calls or JSON schema enforcement for structured outputs - stop is less reliable when the model emits mixed tokens.
- Streaming semantics: we stream via server-sent events (SSE). Each event contains delta pieces of the generated text ("delta":"..."), with occasional "role" and "function_call" events when relevant. A final "[DONE]" event indicates completion. For function calls, we stream the function name and arguments incrementally and then a final event.
- Implementation note: handle partial JSON when streaming structured output - wait for the [DONE] event before performing strict schema validation, or buffer the function call payload and validate once complete.

If you'd like, I can prepare a minimal sample using our Python SDK showing: OAuth token use, per-request model hint, a function-calling schema, streamed consumption and final validation, and an embeddings->ANN->rerank pipeline sketch.
